title: Promote Primary & Secondary Domain Controller
subtitle: Windows Server · Active Directory
status: Written training available · Video coming soon
scope: Two new Windows Server (Desktop Experience) virtual machines on VLAN 10, the domain controllers' own segment of an isolated network. The names and addresses are sample values; replace them with your own plan. The steps follow Microsoft documentation and have not been run on your systems, so confirm each result in your own environment.

chapters.title: Give every system a purpose
chapters.outcome: Record the starting configuration, place both controllers on their own segment, and explain what they will do.
chapters.intro: Start by understanding the services you are about to build and where they will live. Then record the names, addresses, and dependencies for two controllers in the same domain.
steps: Prepare two separate VMs

Use new, patched Windows Server installations (Desktop Experience) with console access and the required administrative credentials. Connect both to VLAN 10, the segment reserved for domain controllers; nothing else joins it. Obtain approved media and updates through your established offline process.
Record names and addresses

Rename the servers SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 and restart as needed. Use 10.0.10.10/24 and 10.0.10.11/24 with 10.0.10.1, the core's VLAN 10 address, as the default gateway. Every other segment reaches the controllers only through the core, which denies anything a rule doesn't permit.
Point DC02 at DC01 and check the clocks

Set SBD-DC02's preferred Domain Name System (DNS) server to 10.0.10.10 so it can find the domain when you promote it, and leave it that way; course 1.2 explains the DNS design. Confirm both clocks agree and document the intended internal time source: SBD-DC01, which course 1.3 makes the domain's time source.
chapters.expected: The two names and static addresses match your plan, the default gateway is 10.0.10.1, and SBD-DC02 lists 10.0.10.10 as its DNS server. Record actual time-source output; a configured address alone does not prove time synchronization.
chapters.mistake: Renaming a domain controller later is a separate procedure with its own steps and checks. Set each server's final name and static address before you promote it.
chapters.network: Both controllers are planned on VLAN 10, the domain controllers' own segment. The platform and network exist, but domain services have not been built yet.

control.name: Baseline Configuration
control.body: Start with a record of the intended components and settings. As the build changes, keep that record aligned with what actually exists.
control.question: Which values are design decisions, and which observations show the actual starting state?
control.evidence: A dated build sheet containing hostnames, addresses, segment and gateway, OS builds, and the chosen domain name.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record your VM names, OS builds, addresses, segment and gateway, time source, and any differences from the sample.
checklist: I recorded the two distinct hostnames and static addresses.
I pointed SBD-DC02 at SBD-DC01 and confirmed the isolated network.
I documented the time source and remaining prerequisites.

quiz.prompt: Why set each server's final name and static address before promotion?
answers: Changing them on a domain controller later is a separate procedure
Promotion assigns a name and address automatically
The domain takes its name from the first server's hostname
quiz.feedback: Promotion records the server as a domain controller under its current name. Settle the name and address first; renaming a controller later has its own procedure and checks.

chapters.title: Create the first domain controller
chapters.outcome: Create the sample forest and bring AD DS online on DC01.
chapters.intro: A new forest establishes the directory's initial boundary. Here, sbd.test is a sample domain, not an existing company domain. Follow this path only for a new forest.
steps: Add the server role
On DC01, open Server Manager → Manage → Add Roles and Features. Choose the local server and Active Directory Domain Services, including its management tools.
Create the forest

Select Promote this server to a domain controller, then Add a new forest. Enter sbd.test. Because both controllers run the same Windows Server release, select the highest forest and domain functional levels the wizard offers. Leave the DNS server option selected; the wizard's DNS delegation warning is expected, and course 1.2 explains both. The first controller in a forest is always a global catalog. Enter and confirm a unique Directory Services Restore Mode password on the server.
Review and promote
Review the SBD NetBIOS name, paths, and prerequisite results. Read any warnings, resolve blocking errors, install, and allow the restart. Then inspect the services and domain.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Get-Service NTDS,Netlogon
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON
chapters.expected: The domain is sbd.test with NetBIOS name SBD. NTDS and Netlogon are running, and SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares exist. Investigate missing services or shares before moving on.
chapters.mistake: Installing the AD DS role is only the first part. The promotion wizard creates the domain controller; a completed role installation alone is not a completed forest.
chapters.network: DC01 now hosts the sbd.test domain. DC02 is still planned; no replication relationship is shown yet.

control.name: Configuration Settings
control.body: Record the settings you selected and why. An installation result is useful evidence, but a defensible configuration record also identifies the applicable requirement and any approved exception.
control.question: Why were these domain and functional-level settings chosen?
control.evidence: Promotion settings, prerequisite results, and post-restart domain and service checks. Keep recovery passwords out of the evidence.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record the domain, promotion outcome, service checks, and the file names of your screenshots or saved output. Do not enter passwords.
checklist: I checked the domain name after restart.
I verified NTDS, Netlogon, SYSVOL, and NETLOGON.
I documented configuration choices without recording credentials.

quiz.prompt: What turns an AD DS role installation into a domain controller?
quiz.feedback: Promotion configures the directory role for a new forest or an existing domain. Merely adding the role is insufficient.

chapters.title: Give the domain a second service point
chapters.outcome: Promote DC02 into the existing domain and inspect the replication relationship.
chapters.intro: A second domain controller gives the domain another live service point. Read why this is a standard availability practice, then add DC02 and verify the result.
steps: Reach the existing directory
On DC02, check that DC01 answers at 10.0.10.10 and that both clocks agree before promotion.
Add a controller to this domain

Install the AD DS role and management tools. In the promotion wizard choose Add a domain controller to an existing domain, enter sbd.test, and authenticate with an authorized Domain Admin account. Leave the DNS server and global catalog options selected, leave Read only domain controller unselected, and set the DSRM password securely.
Finish and inspect
Review site placement, replication source, and prerequisite results; install and restart.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * |
  Select-Object HostName, IPv4Address, IsGlobalCatalog
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl SBD-DC02
chapters.expected: Both hostnames appear with the intended addresses and global catalog roles. After initial convergence, replication checks show successful recent attempts and no unresolved replication failures. Inspect errors rather than assuming the restart completed replication.
chapters.mistake: Choosing Add a new forest creates a different directory. For this chapter, DC02 joins the domain established by DC01.
chapters.network: Both controllers serve the sbd.test domain. The animated relationship represents directory replication, not a measured packet capture.

control.name: System Backup
control.body: Use the second controller to discuss the difference between service availability and recoverability. Replication carries current changes, including damaging ones. Protected backups and a tested recovery process remain separate requirements.
control.question: What would happen if an unwanted directory change replicated to both controllers?
control.evidence: Replication results plus a separate record of the backup and recovery requirements still to implement and test.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record both controllers, replication status and collection time, plus any failures or follow-up actions.
checklist: I confirmed DC02 belongs to the same domain.
I inspected recent replication attempts and unresolved errors.
I can explain why replication does not replace a backup.

quiz.prompt: A damaging directory change reaches both controllers. What does that illustrate?
answers: Replication and historical recovery are different capabilities
quiz.feedback: Both controllers can hold the same unwanted change. Recovery requires protected backups and an appropriate, tested recovery procedure.

chapters.title: Ask the domain to prove it works
chapters.outcome: Check each controller's health, replication in both directions, the roles each holds, and its host firewall.
chapters.intro: A service can be running while the domain is unhealthy. Test each controller by name so every result tells you which controller you checked. Capture actual results and failures in your evidence record.
steps: Test each controller

In an elevated PowerShell window on either controller, run DCDiag against SBD-DC01 and then SBD-DC02. Its default tests cover connectivity, advertising, replication, SYSVOL, services, and role holders. Read each test's result, not just the last line.
Check replication both ways

Run the replication summary, then list each controller's inbound partners. Expect recent successful attempts from DC01 to DC02 and from DC02 to DC01, with no failures. If an error appears right after promotion, wait a few minutes and run the checks again; record any error that persists.
Confirm both controllers' roles

List both controllers with their global catalog status, then the operations master (FSMO) role holders; in this build SBD-DC01 holds all five. Confirm SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on SBD-DC02 as well. If they are not, its first SYSVOL replication has not finished.
Confirm the second layer

On each controller, confirm the network profile is DomainAuthenticated and that the effective firewall policy is on for the Domain, Private, and Public profiles and blocks unsolicited inbound connections. A controller that reports the Public or Private profile is applying a different rule set than the domain expects; find out why before you rely on it.
chapters.command:
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC01
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC02
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl *
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object HostName, IsGlobalCatalog
netdom query fsmo
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON -CimSession SBD-DC02
Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, NetworkCategory
Get-NetFirewallProfile -PolicyStore ActiveStore |
  Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction
chapters.expected: Each controller passes its DCDiag tests, or every failure has a recorded cause. Replication shows recent successful attempts in both directions and no failures. Both controllers are global catalogs, SBD-DC01 holds the five operations master roles, SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on both, and each controller reports the DomainAuthenticated profile with every firewall profile on and inbound blocked by default. Save output with host, time, and interpretation; a command that ran is not a pass.
chapters.mistake: A successful ping proves only that an address answers. It doesn't show that the directory replicates, that SYSVOL is shared, or that a controller can authenticate anyone.
chapters.network: Follow a health check from the administration viewpoint to either controller, and switch the target to check the other. The arc between the controllers is the replication you confirm in both directions.

control.name: Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)
control.body: Healthy, replicating controllers are a precondition for organizational users signing in to the domain. These checks show the identity service is in place on both servers; they do not demonstrate every authentication requirement, such as multifactor authentication or account policy.
control.question: What do these checks establish, and what authentication behavior still needs its own test?
control.evidence: DCDiag output for each controller, replication results in both directions, the role list, and a short statement of what was and was not tested.

chapters.evidencePrompt: For each controller, record the DCDiag results, replication status in both directions, the roles it holds, its network profile and firewall state, the test time, and what the results establish.
checklist: I ran DCDiag against SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 separately.
I confirmed replication succeeds in both directions.
I recorded each controller's roles and the limits of these checks.

quiz.prompt: repadmin /replsummary reports no failures. What does that establish?
answers: The most recent replication attempts between the controllers succeeded
The system is authorized to operate
quiz.feedback: The summary describes the latest attempts at that moment. Authentication requirements, recovery, and authorization need their own evidence and decisions.

model.label: Sign in, step 3
model.text: This step depends on the controllers you just verified: the workstation proves its identity to the Key Distribution Center on SBD-DC01.

chapters.title: Leave a build someone else can understand
chapters.outcome: Assemble your configuration record, test evidence, and remaining work.
chapters.intro: The useful deliverable is a build you can explain and check again. Your evidence record connects each action with an observed result and identifies what remains unresolved.
steps: Describe the final state
Record the domain, both controllers, their segment and gateway, site placement, and actual role holders. Preserve the distinction between the intended design and observed configuration.
Keep a small evidence set

Store your environment outputs locally with descriptive filenames and collection times. In this companion, write a short summary and the file references; the form does not upload or collect your screenshots, server output, or credentials.
Plan the next check

List remaining hardening, auditing, backup, recovery, and client-validation work. Assign an owner or next action. Revisit checks after relevant configuration changes. Export the evidence record before moving devices.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomain |
  Select-Object DNSRoot, PDCEmulator, RIDMaster, InfrastructureMaster
Get-ADForest |
  Select-Object RootDomain, SchemaMaster, DomainNamingMaster
chapters.expected: The record identifies the actual role holders and links configuration decisions to dated test results. Open issues remain visible. Lesson completion records learning activity; it is not a system authorization decision.
chapters.mistake: A diagram becoming complete does not establish that your VM passed a check. The model tells the lesson story; your observations establish what happened in your environment.
chapters.network: Both controllers are built and verified for this course. Continue into the full network to see the services that later lessons can add.

foundations.title: What is Active Directory?
foundations.summary: The shared directory behind domain identities.
blocks: A directory for people and computers

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the Windows Server directory service. It stores objects such as user accounts, computer accounts, and groups, together with their attributes. Administrators use this shared directory to organize identities and manage access consistently.
The domain and the controller

A domain is a logical collection of directory objects, named here sbd.test. A domain controller (DC) is a server running AD DS that stores and serves that directory. DC01 and DC02 are two servers serving the same domain. A forest contains one or more domains; this build starts with one.
Identity, permissions, and policy

Authentication checks who is signing in. Authorization determines what that identity may access. Signing in successfully does not grant access to every resource: the destination service still applies its permissions. Groups make it practical to assign access to roles instead of managing every person separately.
Organization and consistent settings

Organizational units (OUs) organize objects and support delegated administration and Group Policy. Group Policy applies centrally managed settings to users and computers. A global catalog helps find directory objects across a forest; both controllers in this course provide that role.
foundations.takeaway: AD DS stores the directory, and every domain controller serves it. Authentication proves who someone is; authorization decides what they may reach.
foundations.prompt: Explain the difference between the sbd.test domain and the SBD-DC01 server.

foundations.title: Where do the controllers live?
foundations.summary: On a segment of their own, behind a core that denies by default.
blocks: A segment reserved for controllers

SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 sit on VLAN 10 (10.0.10.0/24), a segment that holds domain controllers and nothing else. Workstations, member servers, security tools, and administrators sit on segments of their own. The core joins the segments, and its VLAN 10 address, 10.0.10.1, is the controllers' default gateway.
Deny by default, allow by exception

The core denies every session between segments unless a documented rule permits it, and logs what it denies. Members reach the controllers only for name resolution (course 1.2) and the services in "What crosses the network?". Traffic between the two controllers stays inside VLAN 10, so the core never routes it.
Only Tier 0 manages a controller

From other segments, Remote Desktop, PowerShell remoting, and AD Web Services reach a controller only from AdminJumpBox01, the Tier 0 host on VLAN 60 that course 1.8 builds; until then, use the VM console. Members still reach SMB and RPC, which can carry administration too, so Tier 0 accounts never sign in to them.
Two layers, and no internet

Windows Defender Firewall stays on in every profile and blocks what no rule allows, so an unopened port stays closed even if a core rule is wrong. Keep Remote Desktop off. The directory rules accept any address, and the remoting and AD Web Services rules do too until course 1.8 limits them to the Tier 0 host, so the core decides who reaches those ports. No segment routes to the internet; approved media is the only way in.
foundations.takeaway: A controller's segment is part of its security: VLAN 10 for controllers only, default deny at the core, management only from Tier 0, and the host firewall on in every profile.
foundations.prompt: A workstation on VLAN 80 can open Remote Desktop to SBD-DC01. Which two layers failed, and where would you look first?

model.label: VLAN 10
model.text: The domain controllers' segment, with its boundary, both controllers and their addresses, and the controls that apply.

foundations.title: Why use two domain controllers?
foundations.summary: Keep the directory available when one server is unavailable.
blocks: Remove the single-server dependency

With one DC, its outage removes the only live directory service point. With two healthy, reachable controllers, clients can use a surviving DC for supported operations. This also lets you patch or restart one server while the other continues serving requests. Reconnection may take time; uninterrupted service is not guaranteed.
Both controllers do useful work

Both writable DCs can process normal directory changes and authentication requests. Replication shares directory changes between them. “Primary” and “secondary” describe the order you promote them, not a primary server and an idle spare. Certain operations still depend on a single FSMO role holder, so role placement and recovery need their own plan.
Make the redundancy real

Microsoft recommends at least two virtualized DCs per domain on different virtualization hosts. Two VMs on one host share that host as a failure point. Consider shared storage, power, and network dependencies too.
Availability still needs recovery

Replication can spread an accidental deletion or harmful change to both servers. Keep protected backups and test recovery separately. Two is a starting point for this design, not a universal capacity target: additional sites, users, and recovery needs may require more controllers.
foundations.takeaway: Before relying on DC02, verify replication, review shared dependencies, and confirm both controllers pass their health checks.
foundations.prompt: If both controllers run on the same physical host, which outage would still stop both services?

model.label: DC01 is down, step 3
model.text: With SBD-DC01 offline, the workstation authenticates with SBD-DC02 instead, so sign-in continues.

foundations.title: What crosses the network?
foundations.summary: The ports a domain member needs to reach its domain controllers.
blocks: Every conversation crosses the core
Domain members sit on other segments, so each conversation in this table crosses the core, which allows it only because a rule says so. System Hub shows each one crossing the core switch.
Sign-in is only the start

Kerberos proves who is signing in. After that, the member reads the directory over LDAP, pulls Group Policy and scripts from SYSVOL over SMB, and uses RPC for NetLogon. Time matters too: Kerberos rejects clocks that drift too far apart.

table.caption: What crosses the core to the domain controllers, after name resolution (course 1.2)
head: Purpose
Port
What it carries
rows: LDAP and LDAPS; UDP 389 carries the domain controller locator ping
SMB reads of policies and scripts from domain controller shares
Endpoint mapper, then the dynamic range for NetLogon, LSA, and SAM
W32Time; members follow the domain time hierarchy
Remote Desktop, PowerShell remoting, and AD Web Services, only from the Tier 0 administration host

foundations.takeaway: Allowing Kerberos isn't enough. Applying Group Policy and reading SYSVOL also need LDAP, SMB, and RPC. In the System Hub design, rules F02, F03, and F09 permit this profile for domain members, with LDAP signing and channel binding required, and rule A01 limits administration to the Tier 0 host. Name resolution has its own rule (F01), and so does credentialed scanning (F15), which arrives with course 1.17, coming soon; everything else is denied.
